identity.title: On Scaling Up 3D Gaussian Splatting Training

problem.claim: Enable 3D Gaussian Splatting training for high-resolution and large-scale 3D reconstruction beyond single-GPU memory limits.

gap.claim: Existing 3DGS training is described as single-GPU and single-view at a time, limiting parameter scale and batched multi-view training.

contributions.claim: The authors introduce Grendel, which partitions 3DGS parameters and parallelizes computation across multiple GPUs using sparse all-to-all communication and dynamic load balancing.
Grendel supports batched multi-view training and the authors report that square-root batch-size scaling is highly effective for optimization hyperparameters.
The project is released as open source.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors distinguish Grendel from existing 3DGS systems through multi-GPU parameter scaling, sparse communication, dynamic load balancing, and batched multi-view training.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report improved rendering quality on large-scale, high-resolution scenes when 3DGS parameters are scaled across multiple GPUs.
On the 4K Rubble dataset, the authors report test PSNR 27.28 using 40.4 million Gaussians across 16 GPUs, versus 26.28 using 11.2 million Gaussians on one GPU.
The authors report that a square-root batch-size hyperparameter scaling rule is highly effective.

narrative_sequence.summary: 3DGS offers high visual quality and fast rendering, but single-GPU training limits scale because of memory constraints.
The authors introduce Grendel to partition parameters and parallelize computation across GPUs.
Grendel routes dynamically relevant Gaussians with sparse all-to-all communication, balances load dynamically, and enables batched multi-view training.
The authors examine hyperparameter scaling and report square-root batch-size scaling, improved scene rendering quality, and the Rubble PSNR comparison.

source_observation.claim: The abstract pairs a systems bottleneck with a mechanism tailored to sparse, dynamically changing pixel influence, then reports a quality comparison at different GPU and Gaussian counts.

lessons.interpretation: This links the proposed architecture to the stated bottleneck and makes the scale change concrete.
lessons.application: When presenting a scalable system, connect each communication or balancing mechanism to the workload structure and include a direct resource-scale comparison with the reported outcome.
lessons.exception: This framing is less suitable when the workload lacks exploitable sparsity or when resource changes cannot be isolated from other experimental changes.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify training time, memory use, convergence behavior, or comparisons against distributed baselines.
The reported PSNR comparison changes both GPU count and Gaussian count, so the abstract does not isolate the contribution of distribution alone.
Evaluation scope, scene count, and experimental conditions are not provided.
